transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm glad you're here today. What brings you in to see me?

Hi. Thank you. Um, well, what finally pushed me to make an appointment is that I keep getting up when I really shouldn't. Like, during sprint planning for work, or even important personal things like mortgage calls. I know I'm supposed to stay put, but I just... I'll suddenly decide I need a glass of water right then, or I'll get up to check something in the other room. It's frustrating because I know I need to stay in my seat, but I just keep doing it anyway.

When you're sitting in these meetings or on important calls, are you having trouble focusing on what's being said, or do you feel like you understand what's happening but just can't seem to stay in your seat?

I think it's actually a bit of both. I definitely have trouble focusing, too. Like, I'll sit down to review a pull request for work, or read through those mortgage documents, and I start out with really good intentions. But... after just a few minutes, I'll suddenly realize I'm staring at the exact same section. I haven't actually processed any of it because my mind is off thinking about five completely unrelated things.
When did you first notice these problems with focus and staying in your seat? Was this something you've struggled with since childhood, or did it start more recently?

Um, it's definitely something I've struggled with since I was a kid. I actually remember teachers in elementary school having to move my desk, or constantly reminding me to stay seated. I was just always popping up out of my chair. Or I'd be talking before I was actually called on. I'd also rush through things—like my assignments—even when I understood the work perfectly fine. So, yeah, it's not a recent thing at all. It's been going on for a long time.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient presents with lifelong history of inattention, hyperactivity (difficulty staying seated), and impulsivity (interrupting, rushing through tasks) beginning in childhood. Symptoms are pervasive across multiple settings (school, work, personal life) and cause functional impairment. Clinical presentation is consistent with Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder, Combined Type or predominantly hyperactive-impulsive presentation.
